question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int^{-2}_{-\infty} 4e^{x} \,\textrm{d}x &=4\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_a^{-2} e^{x} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=4\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ e^{x} \right]_a^{-2}\\[5pt] &=4\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left(e^{-2}- e^{a} \right)\\[5pt] &= 4\cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{e^2} -\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} e^{a}\right) \end{align*}

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=e^x$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} e^x = 0$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} e^x = \infty$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^{-2} 4e^x \,\textrm{d}x &=4\cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{e^2} -\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} e^{a}\right)\\[5pt] &=4\left( \dfrac{1}{e^2} - 0\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{4}{e^2}}. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, let's recall the following result:

\[ \int e^{px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1p e^{px+q} + C \]

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-3x+2} \,\textrm{d}x &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_{0}^{a} e^{-3x+2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ -\dfrac{1}{3}e^{-3x+2} \right]_{0}^{a}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}e^{-3a+2}+ \dfrac{1}{3}e^{2} \right)\\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{e^2}{3} -\dfrac{e^2}{3}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} e^{-3a}\right) \end{align*}

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=e^{-3x}$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} e^{-3x} = \infty$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} e^{-3x} = 0$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-3x+2} \,\textrm{d}x &= \left(\dfrac{e^2}{3} -\dfrac{e^2}{3}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} e^{-3a}\right)\\[5pt] & =\dfrac{e^2}{3}-\dfrac{e^2}{3}\cdot 0\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{e^2}{3}}. \end{align*}

\begin{align*} \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-4x-3} \,\textrm{d}x &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_{1}^{a} e^{-4x-3} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ -\dfrac{1}{4}e^{-4x-3} \right]_{1}^{a}\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left(-\dfrac{1}{4}e^{-4a-3}+ \dfrac{1}{4}e^{-7} \right)\\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{1}{4e^7} -\dfrac{1}{4e^3}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} e^{-4a}\right) \end{align*}

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=e^{-4x}$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} e^{-4x} = \infty$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} e^{-4x} = 0$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-4x-3} \,\textrm{d}x &= \left(\dfrac{1}{4e^7} -\dfrac{1}{4e^3}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} e^{-4a}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4e^7}-\dfrac{1}{4e^3}\cdot 0\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{4e^7}}. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int^{-1}_{-\infty} \dfrac{3}{4}e^{x} \,\textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{3}{4}\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_a^{-1} e^{x} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{4}\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ e^{x} \right]_a^{-1}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{4}\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left(e^{-1}- e^{a} \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4}\cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{e} -\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} e^{a}\right) \end{align*}

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=e^x$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} e^x = 0$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} e^x = \infty$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^{-1} \dfrac{3}{4}e^x \,\textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{3}{4}\cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{e} -\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} e^{a}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{4}\left( \dfrac{1}{e} - 0\right)\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3}{4e}}. \end{align*}

example.title: Improper Integral Involving the Exponential Function

question.explanation:
First, let's recall the following result:

\[ \int e^{px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1p e^{px+q} + C \]

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_1^\infty e^{-x} \,\textrm{d}x &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_1^a e^{-x} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ - e^{-x}\right]_1^a\\[5pt] &=-\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[e^{-x}\right]_1^a\\[5pt] &= -\left(\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \dfrac{1}{e^{a}} -e^{-1}\right) \end{align*}

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\dfrac{1}{e^x},$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{e^x} = \infty$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{e^x} = 0$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \int_1^\infty e^{-x} \,\textrm{d}x & =-\left(\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \dfrac{1}{e^{a}} -e^{-1}\right) \\[5pt] &=-\left(0-e^{-1}\right) \\[5pt] &=e^{-1}. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^1 2^x \,\textrm{d}x &=\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_a^1 2^x \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac {2^x}{\ln(2)} \right]_a^1\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{\ln(2)} \cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ {2^x} \right]_a^1\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{\ln(2)} \cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left( 2^1 - 2^a\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{\ln(2)} \cdot\left( 2 - \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} 2^a \right) \end{align*}

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=2^x$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} 2^x = 0$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} 2^x = \infty$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^1 2^x \,\textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{1}{\ln(2)} \cdot\left( 2 - \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} 2^a \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{\ln(2)} \cdot \left(2 - 0 \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\ln(2)}. \end{align*}

example.title: Improper Integral Involving Other Exponential Functions

question.explanation:

\[ \int b^{\,px + q}\,\textrm d x = \dfrac1{p\ln(b)} b^{\,px+q} + C \]

We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^0 5^{x/2} \,\textrm{d}x &=\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_a^0 5^{x/2} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac {2\cdot 5^{x/2}}{\ln(5)} \right]_a^0\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\ln(5)} \cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ 5^{x/2} \right]_a^0\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\ln(5)} \cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left( 1 - 5^{a/2}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\ln(5)} \cdot\left( 1 - \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} 5^{a/2} \right) \end{align*}

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=5^{x/2}$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} 5^{x/2} = 0$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} 5^{x/2} = \infty$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^0 5^{x/2} \,\textrm{d}x &=\dfrac{2}{\ln(5)} \cdot\left( 1 - \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} 5^{a/2} \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\ln(5)} \cdot \left(1 - 0 \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\ln(5)}. \end{align*}

\begin{align*} \int_{-\infty}^{1} 3^{2x-1} \,\textrm{d}x &=\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \int_a^{1} 3^{2x-1} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ \dfrac {3^{2x-1}} {2\ln(3)} \right]_a^{1}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3^{-1}}{2\ln(3)}\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} \left[ 3^{2x} \right]_a^{1}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{6\ln(3)}\cdot\left( 3^{2} - \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} {3^{2a}} \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{6\ln(3)}\cdot\left(9 - \lim_{a\rightarrow-\infty} {3^{2a}} \right) \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution

question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=x^2.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u =2x\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $ u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x^2$ is as follows:

$x$ $0$ $\infty$
$u$ $0$ $\infty$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\[ \displaystyle\int_0^{\infty} 2x\cdot7^{-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x =\int_0^{\infty} 7^{-u} \,\textrm{d}u . \]

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

\begin{align*} \int_0^{\infty} 2x\cdot 7^{-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x&=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_0^a 7^{-u} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[ - \dfrac{7^{-u}}{\ln 7} \right]_0^{a} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 1{\ln 7}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty}\big[ 7^{-u} \big]_0^{a} \\[5pt] &=-\dfrac 1{\ln 7}\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left( \dfrac{1}{7^{a}} -1 \right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac 1{\ln 7}\left(1-\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \dfrac{1}{7^{a}} \right) \end{align*}

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\dfrac{1}{7^x},$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{7^x} = \infty$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{7^x} = 0$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \int_0^\infty 2x\cdot7^{-x^2} \,\textrm{d}x &=\dfrac 1{\ln 7}\left(1-\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \dfrac{1}{7^{a}} \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac 1{\ln 7}\left(1-0 \right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac 1{\ln 7}. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=\ln x.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{1}{{x}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}u =\dfrac{1}{{x}}\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $ u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\ln x$ is as follows:

$x$ $1$ $\infty$
$u$ $0$ $\infty$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is \begin{align} \displaystyle \int_1^\infty \dfrac{1}{x\cdot 4^{\ln x}} \,\textrm{d}x &=\int_0^\infty \dfrac1{4^u} \,\textrm{d}u=\int_0^\infty 4^{-u} \,\textrm{d}u. \end{align}

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_1^\infty \dfrac{1}{x\cdot 4^{\ln x}} \,\textrm{d}x &=\int_0^\infty 4^{-u} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_0^a {4^{-u}} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[-\dfrac{4^{-u}}{\ln 4} \right]_0^a\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{1}{\ln 4}\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[4^{-u} \right]_0^a\\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 1{\ln 4}\cdot \left(\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \dfrac1{4^{a}}- 1 \right)\\[5pt] \end{align*}

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\dfrac{1}{4^x},$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{4^x} = \infty$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{4^x} = 0$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_1^\infty \dfrac{1}{x\cdot 4^{\ln x}} \,\textrm{d}x &=-\dfrac 1{\ln 4}\cdot \left(\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \dfrac1{4^{a}}- 1 \right)\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac 1{\ln 4}\cdot \left(0- 1 \right)\\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac 1{\ln 4}}. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u = \dfrac{1}{x}.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = -\dfrac{1}{x^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\textrm{d}u = \dfrac{1}{x^2}\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $u \to -\infty$ when $x \to 0^-$ and $u \to 0$ when $x \to -\infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u = \dfrac{1}{x}$ is as follows:

$x$ $0$ $-\infty$
$u$ $-\infty$ $0$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is \[ \displaystyle\int^0_{-\infty} \dfrac{e^{3/x - 1}}{x^2} \,\textrm{d}x = -\int_0^{-\infty} e^{3u - 1} \,\textrm{d}u = \int_{-\infty}^0 e^{3u - 1} \,\textrm{d}u. \]

Now, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a \to -\infty.$ \begin{align*} \int^0_{-\infty} \dfrac{e^{3/x - 1}}{x^2} \,\textrm{d}x &= \lim_{a \rightarrow -\infty} \int_a^0 e^{3u - 1} \,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \lim_{a \rightarrow -\infty} \left[\dfrac{e^{3u - 1}}{3}\right]_{a}^0 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3}\lim_{a \rightarrow -\infty} \left(e^{-1} - e^{3a - 1}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-1}}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}\lim_{a \rightarrow -\infty} e^{3a - 1} \end{align*}

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y = e^{3x - 1}$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow -\infty} e^{3x - 1} = 0$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \infty} e^{3x - 1} = \infty$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that \begin{align*} \int^0_{-\infty} \dfrac{e^{3/x - 1}}{x^2} \,\textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{e^{-1}}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3}\lim_{a \rightarrow -\infty} e^{3a - 1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^{-1}}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot 0 \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{1}{3e}}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating an Improper Integral Using a Substitution

question.explanation:
First, we substitute $u=\sqrt x.$ Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2\textrm{d}u =\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\textrm{d}x. \]

Since $ u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\sqrt x$ is as follows:

$x$ $0$ $\infty$
$u$ $0$ $\infty$

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

\begin{align} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{3^{-\sqrt x}}{\sqrt{x}} \,\textrm{d}x &=2 \int_0^\infty 3^{-u} \,\textrm{d}u. \end{align}

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{3^{-\sqrt x}}{\sqrt{x}} \,\textrm{d}x &=2\int_0^\infty 3^{-u} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=2\cdot\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \int_0^a {3^{-u}} \,\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=2\cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[-\dfrac{{3^{-u}}}{\ln 3} \right]_0^a\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{2}{\ln 3} \cdot \lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \left[3^{-u} \right]_0^a\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{2}{\ln 3} \cdot \left(\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \dfrac{1}{3^{a}}-1 \right) \end{align*}

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\dfrac{1}{3^{x}},$ shown in the graph below:

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to -\infty} \dfrac{1}{3^{x}} = \infty$

  • $\lim\limits_{x \to \infty} \dfrac{1}{3^{x}} = 0$

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \int_0^\infty \dfrac{3^{-\sqrt x}}{\sqrt{x}} \,\textrm{d}x &=-\dfrac{2}{\ln 3} \cdot \left(\lim_{a\rightarrow\infty} \dfrac{1}{3^{a}}-1 \right)\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{2}{\ln 3} \cdot \left(0-1 \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\ln 3}. \end{align*}
